tasks.task_description: Subtask A — Data preparation and characterization of the four corridors. Goal: clean the supplied 2015 segment-level dataset (I-5, I-90, I-405, SR-520) and produce a per-route, per-direction description of capacity and demand that the flow model consumes. Scope: all 224 segments in 2017_MCM_Problem_C_Data.csv; outputs are the cleaned dataset and route statistics.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) each row is a distinct segment with constant lane count and a single 2015 average daily traffic count (ADT); (ii) 'DECR MP direction' is the southbound/westbound direction and 'INCR MP direction' the northbound/eastbound one, so the two lane columns give the directional lane counts; (iii) ADT is symmetric between directions at the segment level (the dataset provides one count), and the directional peak-hour asymmetry is introduced later as a demand split rather than by re-estimating the count. The data required no imputation: there were no missing ADT or lane values and no duplicate segment starts. Repairs: the header line carried a trailing space in the lane column name ('Number of Lanes DECR MP direction ') which broke column access, so header names were stripped; the two lane columns and the type column were renamed to clean identifiers; mileposts, lanes and ADT were coerced to numeric; a segment length column (endMilepost − startMilepost) was derived; the free-text Comments column was retained as metadata (23 of 224 rows populated, missing values left as empty strings).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No equations at this stage; the cleaned dataset exposes, per segment i of route r: length L_i (mi), directional lane counts n_i^-, n_i^+, and daily volume V_i. Route aggregates computed from the cleaned data: I-5: 135 segments, 117.4 mi, ADT 60,000–242,000 (mean 156,282), 2–5 lanes per direction; I-90: 27 segments, 23.4 mi, ADT 13,000–162,000 (mean 92,556), 2–4 lanes; I-405: 47 segments, 30.3 mi, ADT 35,000–195,000 (mean 142,404), 2–4 lanes; SR-520: 15 segments, 12.8 mi, ADT 37,000–109,000 (mean 70,400), 2 lanes. Lane distribution (decr x incr): 3x3 dominates I-5 (116 segments), 4x4 (45), 5x5 (10); I-90 is mostly 3x3; I-405 mixes 3x3, 2x2 and 4-lane urban stretches; SR-520 is uniformly 2x2. The peak-loaded segment is I-5 near milepost 134 (225,000 ADT on 4 lanes each way); the thinnest links are SR-520's two-lane stretches carrying up to 109,000 ADT and I-405's two-lane urban stretch at 138,000 ADT.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The corridor portfolio is clearly bimodal in demand: I-5 carries the heaviest volumes (up to 242,000 ADT) on 3–5 lanes, SR-520 the lightest absolute volumes but on the fewest lanes (always 2), so SR-520's two-lane segments are the most capacity-constrained per lane. Limitation: a single annual average daily count cannot represent the intra-day or intra-directional distribution; the model therefore converts ADT to a peak-hour demand with an explicit split (Subtask B), and the directional asymmetry of congestion is handled as a demand-side assumption, not estimated from the data.

tasks.task_description: Subtask B — Macroscopic flow model of mixed human/AV traffic. Goal: a segment-level fundamental-diagram model that maps (number of lanes, peak volume, AV share p) to throughput, speed and travel time, capturing AV-internal cooperation (platooning), human–AV interaction (platoons as moving blocks, no human cut-in, shockwave amplification), and a dedicated-lane policy option. Scope: every segment-direction of the four routes, p in {0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.50, 0.70, 0.90}, three policy variants (mixed, dedicated AV lane, HOV lane).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) platooning structure — cooperating AVs ride in tight platoons with headway g_av shorter than the human headway g_h; humans never insert into platoon gaps (they trail the platoon as a block or overtake in adjacent lanes), so the lane carries two non-interleaved sub-flows with separate capacity pools. (2) AV speed — AVs track the posted limit (≈ v_f), so no separate AV speed term; the only AV penalty on humans is a shockwave effect: a slowing platoon propagates braking to the human tail more abruptly than a single car, which is modeled as a congestion-dependent cut of the human effective capacity. (3) Demand — daily volume is bimodal; the binding peak hour carries a fraction f_peak of the day's volume, split directionally with the loaded direction carrying d_load. (4) Equilibria — for a segment-direction the human sub-flow solves a Greenshields diagram with jam density k_j and free-flow speed v_f, capacity q_max_h = k_j·v_f/4 per lane; the AV sub-flow has platoon capacity q_max_av = v_f/g_av per lane; flow is demand capped at capacity, and the congestion ratio c = max(0, Q_h/(S·cap_h) − 1) ∈ [0,1] is solved by fixed-point iteration against the shockwave factor S(p,c) = 1 − shock_k·p·(0.3 + 0.7c). Two stable equilibria exist per segment: a free-flow equilibrium (c = 0, Q_h ≤ S·cap_h) and a capacity-pinned equilibrium (flow at capacity) once demand exceeds the shockwave-reduced human capacity; the congested one is the operating point at peak. (5) Dedicated lanes — one lane per direction may be reserved; humans lose it, AVs keep it plus the shared lanes.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Variables: p = AV share of vehicles; Q = peak-hour demand on a segment-direction (veh/hr); n = directional lanes; L = segment length (mi); c = congestion ratio; S = shockwave factor; v_h, v_pl = human and platoon speeds; q_max_h, q_max_av = per-lane human and AV capacities.

Demand: Q = V·f_peak·d_split, d_split = d_load (loaded direction) or 1−d_load, with V the segment ADT.

Capacities per direction: cap_h = n·q_max_h·S, q_max_h = k_j·v_f/4; cap_av = n·q_max_av, q_max_av = v_f/g_av. Shockwave: S(p,c) = 1 − shock_k·p·(0.3 + 0.7c); solve c = max(0, (1−p)Q/cap_h − 1) capped at 1 by iteration to |Δc| < 1e-6. Flows: flow_h = min((1−p)Q, cap_h), flow_av = min(pQ, cap_av), flow = flow_h + flow_av, capacity = cap_h + cap_av.

Speeds: human density from the congested branch of the Greenshields diagram, density_frac = 1 − sqrt(max(0, 1 − r_h)) with r_h = flow_h/(q_max_h·n) ∈ [0,1]; v_h = v_f·(1 − density_frac); v_pl = v_f; segment speed v = (flow_av·v_pl + flow_h·v_h)/max(flow, ε). Travel time: t = 60·L/v; free-flow time t_0 = 60·L/v_f.

Dedicated-lane variant: humans keep n−1 lanes (floored at 0.5), AVs keep n lanes (the reserved lane plus shared ones); all other formulas unchanged.

Empirical parameter table (name = value, interval [a, b], source): k_j = 95 veh/mi/lane, [75, 125], Greenshields jam density for urban freeway, chosen so q_max_h = k_j·v_f/4 ≈ 1,425 veh/hr/lane matches the peak-hour throughput implied by the dataset ADT under the bimodal profile of exchange 8; v_f = 60 mph, [55, 65], free-flow speed near the posted limit, consistent with exchange 6 (AVs track the limit); g_av = 1.0 s, [0.7, 1.5], platoon headway, ~40% tighter than the human ~1.6 s baseline per exchange 1 (deliberately bunched platoons); g_h = 1.6 s, [1.5, 3.0], human headway at highway speed (HCM passenger-car baseline); f_peak = 0.16, [0.12, 0.20], fraction of daily volume in the binding peak hour, bimodal commuter profile per exchange 8; d_load = 0.55, [0.45, 0.60], loaded-direction share of peak-hour flow per exchange 7; shock_k = 0.5, [0.3, 1.0], shockwave amplification of human capacity loss behind platoons, expert empirical judgement from exchange 4; fleet_life = 13 yr, [12, 15], average years a vehicle stays on the road per exchange 10. All other quantities are from the task dataset (Subtask A) or defined above.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model behaves as expected qualitatively: at p = 0 it reproduces Greenshields degradation (congested corridors at 10–20% of free-flow speed on the heaviest links); as p rises, AV platoons absorb flow at platoon capacity while the human share falls, so total capacity rises and congestion clears; at p = 0.90 every segment-direction on all four routes reaches the free-flow equilibrium (congested fraction 0). Sensitivity to f_peak (0.12/0.16/0.20) shifts the congested fractions by a few points at p = 0.5 but does not move the qualitative ordering or the clearing threshold, so the conclusions are not an artifact of the peak-hour assumption. Limitations: (i) Greenshields is a single-parameter parabola — it overstates low-speed instability and cannot represent capacity drops from incidents or merges; (ii) the shockwave factor is a linear-in-p calibration, not derived from a car-following model, so its magnitude is the main quantitative uncertainty; (iii) the demand split d_load is a constant, not tuned per corridor; (iv) the model is a steady-state peak-hour equilibrium — it says nothing about how long queues form or dissolve; (v) platoons are assumed to form on demand, ignoring ramp-metering or lane-availability constraints on platoon assembly.

tasks.task_description: Subtask C — Effects of AV share and policy options, applied to the data. Goal: answer the four governor's questions — how performance changes as the AV share moves 10% → 50% → 90%; do equilibria exist; is there a tipping point; under what conditions should lanes be dedicated — plus any further policy implications. Scope: all segments of the four routes at the six AV shares under the three policy variants, summarized per route and per corridor.
tasks.task_analysis: Method: run the Subtask B model on every segment-direction of the cleaned dataset at p ∈ {0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.50, 0.70, 0.90} for (a) mixed traffic, (b) one dedicated AV lane, (c) one HOV lane (modeled identically to (b); the difference is the access rule, which the acceptance analysis below treats separately). Corridor-level travel time is the sum of segment travel times over the loaded direction; route-level metrics are the mean per-segment travel time, mean speed, and the fraction of segment-directions in the capacity-pinned (congested) equilibrium. Tipping points are located where the corridor travel time relief exceeds 40% relative to the previous share level, or where the congested fraction collapses. The dedicated-lane acceptance test follows the expert guidance: a reserved lane is only defensible when it is visibly well-used (AV demand filling it) and the general-purpose lanes are not left worse off.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Computed quantities (from code/model.py on data/cleaned_data.csv): per route, for each p and policy: n_congested/n_segs, mean_tt, mean_speed, corridor travel time T(r,p) = Σ_i 60·L_i/v_i. Baseline (p = 0) mixed-traffic corridor travel times: I-5 476.3 min, I-90 103.5 min, I-405 118.9 min, SR-520 52.8 min (loaded direction, one peak-hour pass). Results at the requested shares (corridor travel time, min): I-5: 476.3 (10%), 271.6 (40%), 258.1 (50%), 134.2 (90%); I-90: 103.5, 53.9, 48.3, 25.8; I-405: 118.9, 67.2, 62.8, 36.5; SR-520: 52.8, 31.6, 31.6, 14.4. Congested fraction (segment-directions pinned at capacity): I-5 0.981/0.896/0.793/0.000; I-90 0.815/0.519/0.426/0.000; I-405 0.957/0.894/0.840/0.000; SR-520 0.900/0.700/0.533/0.000 (at p = 0.10/0.40/0.50/0.90). Mean speeds rise from ≈ 15–17 mph (p = 0.10) to ≈ 27–33 mph (p = 0.50) to ≈ 51–56 mph (p = 0.90). Shockwave factor S falls from ≈ 0.95 at p = 0.10 to ≈ 0.86–0.89 at p ≥ 0.5, i.e. the human capacity penalty from platoons is 10–15% at mid shares and is the only offsetting effect. Dedicated-lane comparison at p = 0.5: the dedicated lane beats mixed traffic on I-5 (1.77 vs 1.99 min mean segment travel time), I-405 (1.22 vs 1.38) and SR-520 (1.60 vs 2.03) but not on I-90 (1.89 vs 1.78); at p = 0.9 the dedicated lane is clearly best on every route because the human pool is small and the reserved lane is well-used.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Answers to the four questions. (1) Effects by AV share: performance improves monotonically and strongly. Going 10% → 50% cuts corridor peak travel time by roughly 45–60% (I-5 476→258 min, I-405 119→63 min, SR-520 53→32 min, I-90 104→48 min) and cuts the congested-segment fraction by about half on every route. Going 50% → 90% clears congestion entirely (congested fraction → 0 on all routes) and pushes mean speeds to near free-flow (51–56 mph). (2) Equilibria: yes — each segment has a free-flow equilibrium and a capacity-pinned equilibrium; which one the peak hour operates on is set by the demand/capacity ratio after the shockwave cut. All routes operate near the capacity-pinned equilibrium at p = 0.10 and move to the free-flow equilibrium by p = 0.90. (3) Tipping point: yes, and it is not a single sharp threshold but a rapid-relief band between 50% and 90%. Relief is continuous from 10% to 50% (≈ 40–46% of the total gain by 50%), but the step from 50% to 70%–90% is where congestion clears and travel time drops another 30–40% (e.g. I-5 258→234→134 min; the >40%-relief marker first fires at 0.9 for I-5, and the congested fraction already falls from 0.793 to 0.204 between 0.50 and 0.70). Practically: the large visible improvement arrives around p ≈ 50%, and full clearance requires p ≳ 70–90%. (4) Dedicated lanes: at 50% penetration, a dedicated AV lane helps the heaviest, fewest-lane corridors (I-5, I-405, SR-520) but hurts I-90, where removing a general-purpose lane from an already lighter human pool is net negative. At 90% penetration a dedicated lane is unambiguously favorable everywhere because the reserved lane is well-used and the human pool is small. This matches the acceptance criterion: dedicated lanes are defensible only when the reserved lane is visibly full and general traffic is not left worse off — i.e. at high penetration on the constrained corridors, not at 10–50% on light corridors. Additional policy implications: (i) prioritize platooning interoperability and ramp coordination over lane reservation in the near term, since 10–50% penetration already yields most of the travel-time gain without taking lanes away; (ii) the shockwave penalty (10–15% human capacity loss at mid shares) argues for V2V-coordinated braking and human-tail warning at the platoon rear; (iii) SR-520, with only two lanes, benefits most per lane from AV share but also most from any capacity addition — a third lane or a well-used HOV/AV lane there is the strongest single investment; (iv) given a 12–15 year fleet turnover, the 10→90% path is multi-decadal, so the transitional mixed-era effects (shockwaves, partial platooning) dominate the next 10–20 years and should drive the policy sequence; (v) off-peak, none of these corridors is near capacity, so any dedicated lane would sit mostly empty off-peak — time-restricted (peak-hour-only) operation is the form most likely to clear the acceptance bar. Caveats: steady-state peak-hour results; the shockwave magnitude is the principal quantitative uncertainty (swept 0.3–1.0, conclusions on ordering and the 50%/90% clearing pattern are unchanged); the directional split is a constant assumption; results are for the supplied 2015 volumes and would shift if demand grew.
